title: No inventory of AI tools in use
summary: No record exists of which AI systems, models, agents, or AI-backed SaaS features are operating in the environment, by whom, or against which data.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Stand up a single AI asset register before tooling. Four columns is enough at this stage: tool name, data classification accessed, human owner, approved or not. Front any sanctioned LLM calls through a logging gateway so usage is at least observable. LiteLLM and Open WebUI are the common OSS starting points; both can sit between users/apps and any model provider.

aws_bedrock.summary: Stand up the inventory across two AWS surfaces. For managed services: enable Bedrock model invocation logging to CloudWatch and capture model access via CloudTrail data events. For shadow agents and SaaS-installed assistants: use IAM Access Analyzer and AWS Config conformance packs to catch unexpected Bedrock identities.

azure_foundry.summary: Build the register from three surfaces: Foundry project and model deployment resources in the subscription, Defender for Cloud AI security posture for deployments nobody declared, and Purview DSPM for AI for Copilot and third-party assistant usage. Turn on diagnostic settings per Foundry resource so invocations land in a Log Analytics workspace.

links.label: Defender for Cloud AI security posture

google_vertex_ai.summary: Inventory from two sources: the model deployments and endpoints in each project, and Security Command Center asset inventory for resources created outside approved projects. Enable Data Access audit logs so invocation is recorded, not only resource creation.

title: No understanding of AI-specific threats
summary: The security team cannot describe what prompt injection, data exfiltration via model output, model inversion, training-data poisoning, or model extraction look like in the organization's environment.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Read the OWASP AI Exchange threat sections (2 through 4) and the MITRE ATLAS matrix together. Both are vendor-neutral and free. For hands-on practice, run Garak against any LLM you can hit, including hosted endpoints.

aws_bedrock.summary: Use the AWS Generative AI Security Scoping Matrix as the starting threat-awareness reference; it categorizes AI risks by deployment pattern (consumer SaaS, enterprise SaaS, foundation model, customized model, self-trained).

links.label: AWS Generative AI Security Scoping Matrix

azure_foundry.summary: Microsoft's AI Red Team guidance and the Foundry risk and safety evaluators name the same threat classes in product terms, which makes them usable as a team reading list without a subscription.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Google's Secure AI Framework is the vendor-neutral read. Model Armor's documentation names the concrete attack classes it screens for (prompt injection, jailbreak, sensitive data disclosure), which grounds the abstract threats in something testable.

title: Any internal AI/ML models are unprotected
summary: Internal models, training data, and inference endpoints have no access controls, monitoring, or threat modeling beyond whatever the underlying compute happens to provide.

cloud_agnostic.summary: If you have any internal models or fine-tunes, treat them like production code: store weights in artifact storage with access logging, never serve directly from a developer workstation, put inference behind an authenticated proxy, and tag every endpoint as Confidential or Internal in the asset register.

aws_bedrock.summary: Custom models live in SageMaker. Put them in a private VPC, attach a SageMaker Model Registry with approval gating, and front inference endpoints with VPC endpoints rather than public URLs.

azure_foundry.summary: Custom models live in Azure ML. Register every model in the workspace registry, enable customer-managed keys on the workspace, and expose inference through a private endpoint rather than a public scoring URI.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Register custom models in Model Registry, encrypt platform resources with CMEK, and put the project inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter so endpoints are unreachable from outside it.

title: No visibility into the AI supply chain
summary: Models, datasets, and AI-enabled libraries enter the environment without provenance, signature verification, or vendor risk review.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Treat models like dependencies. Pin model identifiers, capture a hash, and require a documented source URL for every model entering the environment. ModelScan and picklescan catch the most common pickle-format risks in Hugging Face artifacts.

aws_bedrock.summary: Prefer Bedrock Marketplace and SageMaker JumpStart for third-party models; both record source, license, and version in account-scoped registries. Block direct downloads from public model hubs at the VPC egress proxy.

azure_foundry.summary: Source models from the Foundry model catalog, which records publisher, license, and version per model. Block egress to public model hubs so an uncatalogued model cannot arrive at run time.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Model Garden is the controlled entry point and carries publisher and license per model. A VPC Service Controls perimeter stops training jobs pulling weights from arbitrary external hosts.

title: Developers pulling models from Hugging Face or similar repositories without verification
summary: Engineers download pretrained weights ad hoc, often in pickle formats, with no verification step. Pickle files can execute arbitrary code on load.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Prefer safetensors over pickle. Scan any pickle artifact before load. Mirror approved models into an internal registry so downloads do not happen at run time from arbitrary external hosts.

links.label: MITRE ATLAS: ML Supply Chain Compromise

aws_bedrock.summary: Use JumpStart or Marketplace as the canonical model source. If a use case demands a Hugging Face model not in JumpStart, mirror through a controlled S3 bucket after pickle-scanning; never let SageMaker training jobs download from public hubs at run time.

azure_foundry.summary: Use the Foundry catalog as the canonical source. When a use case needs a model that is not catalogued, mirror it into an Azure ML registry after scanning and pin the deployment to the registered version.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Deploy from Model Garden rather than a notebook download. Anything mirrored in gets scanned, registered with a version, and gated at deploy time with Binary Authorization on the serving container.

title: No visibility into third-party AI agents or plugins granted access to corporate environments
summary: OAuth-installed agents, browser extensions, and AI-augmented SaaS plugins reach corporate data without an inventory or access review.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Pull OAuth grant logs from your identity provider and list every third-party app with read access to mail, docs, or chat. Revoke anything that no owner can name. Repeat monthly until BYOAI surface is bounded.

links.label: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Apps (LLM06: Excessive Agency)

aws_bedrock.summary: Audit IAM identities with `bedrock:InvokeModel` or `bedrock-agent:*` through IAM Access Analyzer. Any identity outside the AI inventory is a candidate for removal or onboarding.

azure_foundry.summary: Entra enterprise applications lists every OAuth-consented third-party app and the Graph scopes it holds; Purview DSPM for AI adds the assistants touching Microsoft 365 data. Revoke any grant with no named owner.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Review service accounts and their role bindings per project, and replace exported keys with workload identity federation for any external agent. Security Command Center flags over-permissioned identities.

title: No AI/ML used in security tools or operations
summary: Detection, triage, and response are entirely rules-based or human-driven. Vendor AI features in existing tools are either absent or disabled.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Audit the SIEM/EDR/SOAR you already pay for. Vendor-shipped ML detections (UEBA modules, anomaly baselines) are the cheapest first step. Enable them at vendor defaults, document the change, and reassess in 30 days.

aws_bedrock.summary: Turn on the AWS security services that already ship ML detections: GuardDuty (with all data sources enabled), Macie, and Inspector. Pipe Security Hub findings into a single review.

azure_foundry.summary: Defender for Cloud and Sentinel both ship ML detections that are off or unconfigured by default. Enable the Defender for Cloud AI workload plan and Sentinel's built-in anomaly analytics rules, then reassess in 30 days.

links.label: Defender for Cloud AI threat protection

google_vertex_ai.summary: Security Command Center ships built-in anomaly and threat detectors and Google SecOps carries the analytics layer. Turn both on at defaults first, then measure before tuning.

title: The security team is unaware of available AI capabilities
summary: Security engineers cannot describe what AI features their existing tools ship with, what they cost, or what they would change if enabled.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Have each tool owner produce a one-page brief on the AI features in their product, default state (on/off), tier dependency, and known false-positive behavior. Compile into an internal index.

aws_bedrock.summary: AWS Skill Builder has a free generative AI learning plan and a paid security path. Set a baseline expectation that at least one engineer per security domain completes it.

azure_foundry.summary: The Well-Architected AI workload guidance and the Cloud Adoption Framework AI strategy content are the platform's own inventory of what is available and what it costs. Use them as the source for the per-tool briefs.

google_vertex_ai.summary: The Architecture Framework security pillar covers the AI-relevant platform controls in one place, which is the shortest path to a team that can name what it already has.

title: Manual processes dominate detection and response
summary: Alerts are triaged by hand, with no automated enrichment, no model-assisted classification, and no playbook automation.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Capture the top 10 alerts by volume and time-to-disposition. Anything routine and high-volume is a candidate for automation before AI: SOAR-style playbooks first, model-assisted triage later when there is baseline data to evaluate it against.

aws_bedrock.summary: Wire EventBridge rules off Security Hub findings into Step Functions or Lambda for automated triage of routine alert classes (e.g., GuardDuty IAM finding categories).

links.label: Security Hub automated response with EventBridge

azure_foundry.summary: Sentinel automation rules and Logic Apps playbooks take the routine alert classes before any model-assisted triage. Start with the highest-volume analytics rule and measure time-to-disposition.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Google SecOps playbooks automate the high-volume detection classes, with Security Command Center findings as the trigger source.

title: No AI usage policy exists
summary: There is no written policy stating which AI tools are permitted, what data can be entered, or who owns AI decisions.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Draft a one-page AI acceptable use policy in week one. State sanctioned tools, prohibited tools, what data classes can be entered into each, the policy owner, and the consequence model. Publish it, attest it, and revisit in 90 days. Policy precision improves with usage data; do not block on perfection.

aws_bedrock.summary: Add an SCP at the organization root that denies all `bedrock:*` actions outside designated accounts. That forces every AI use case to ride through an approved account where logging and policy apply.

azure_foundry.summary: Azure Policy assigned at the management group denies creation of Foundry and Azure OpenAI resources outside approved subscriptions. That turns the written policy into something structural rather than advisory.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Organization policy constraints restrict which services and regions can be used, so AI resources can only exist in approved projects.

title: BYOAI proliferates unchecked
summary: Employees use personal or unapproved AI tools (ChatGPT, Claude.ai, Gemini, niche assistants) for work tasks. There is no policy to call this Shadow AI; it is BYOAI.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Run a BYOAI discovery survey before blocking. Anonymous, opt-in, listing tools and use cases. Pair with egress log review for known AI domains. The output is a sanctioned list and a remediation list; not a punishment list.

aws_bedrock.summary: An SCP that allows `bedrock:InvokeModel` only for approved model IDs is the structural enforcement; pair with a Bedrock model-invocation logging policy so even allowed use is observable.

azure_foundry.summary: Purview DSPM for AI reports which users are sending data to Copilot and to third-party AI sites, which is the discovery input. Conditional Access then scopes who can reach the sanctioned apps.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Organization policy plus a curated AI-domain list over Cloud Audit Logs gives the same discovery picture: what is sanctioned, what is in use, and what is neither.

title: No visibility into what AI tools employees are using
summary: There is no log of AI domain access, no DLP rule for AI endpoints, and no integration between identity and AI usage.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Start with egress logs. Most networks see AI tool access concentrated in a small set of domains. A weekly report of top AI domains by user (or by department) is enough to start governing. CASB or SASE products extend this with policy at the proxy.

aws_bedrock.summary: VPC Flow Logs plus a curated AI-domain enrichment list in your SIEM gives department-level visibility into external AI tool usage. For Bedrock-internal traffic, model invocation logs cover the same need.

azure_foundry.summary: Purview DSPM for AI is the first-party view of AI usage across Microsoft 365 and connected assistants; Purview Audit holds the underlying activity records for per-department reporting.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Cloud Audit Logs with Data Access logs enabled record every model invocation. Route them into Google SecOps for per-department reporting rather than reading them per project.

title: No AI risk assessment has been conducted
summary: AI risk is not on the enterprise risk register, is not scored, and is not reviewed in any cadence.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Use the OWASP AI Exchange risk-analysis decision tree as the starting framework. Add a single AI line to the enterprise risk register naming the top three threats your organization plausibly faces (almost certainly: data exfiltration, vendor lock-in or outage, regulatory exposure).

aws_bedrock.summary: AWS Audit Manager has a Generative AI Best Practices framework that exposes a starting set of controls and evidence collectors. The framework alone is not a risk assessment, but it makes the gaps explicit.

azure_foundry.summary: The Well-Architected AI workload guidance gives the control set to assess against, and the Azure OpenAI transparency note gives the documented limitations to assess for.

google_vertex_ai.summary: The Architecture Framework security pillar and the platform's responsible AI documentation give the control set; Security Command Center posture findings show where the current gaps are.

title: Leadership unaware of AI exposure
summary: Executives cannot answer 'how much of our data has been sent to public AI models in the last quarter?' or 'who owns AI decisions here?'

cloud_agnostic.summary: Brief leadership with two numbers and one named owner: number of AI tools in the inventory, percentage of staff who have touched one in the last 30 days (egress log estimate is fine), and the named AI governance lead. The point of the brief is to anchor accountability, not to recommend tooling.

aws_bedrock.summary: Cost Explorer tagged by service surfaces Bedrock and SageMaker spend trend lines that translate well to executive briefs. Pair with a count of distinct IAM identities invoking Bedrock per month.

azure_foundry.summary: Cost analysis filtered to the AI services gives the spend trend and Purview DSPM for AI gives the user count. Those two numbers plus a named owner are the brief.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Billing budgets and reports scoped to the AI services give the spend line; audit logs give distinct callers per month.

title: No distinction is made between conversational AI and action-taking AI
summary: Policy and threat modeling treat chatbots and agentic systems identically, ignoring that agents can invoke functions, send mail, write code, and authorize transactions.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Add a single sentence to the policy: 'AI that can take actions on systems requires explicit security review before deployment, separate from conversational AI.' That sentence does most of the work at Stage 1. Implementation comes at Stage 3.

links.label: OWASP Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock distinguishes model invocation (InvokeModel) from agentic action (Agents for Bedrock and AgentCore). Treat any role with `bedrock-agent:*` permissions as agentic in your policy.

azure_foundry.summary: Foundry separates model inference from the Agent Service. Treat any identity with a role on the Agent Service, its tools, or its connections as agentic in the policy.

google_vertex_ai.summary: The platform separates model inference from the agent runtime. Any service account attached to an agent deployment is agentic and takes the stricter review path.

title: Inventory of sanctioned AI tools exists but may be incomplete
summary: A list of approved AI tools is maintained but rarely reconciled against actual usage. Shadow AI is suspected but unmeasured.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Reconcile the inventory against actual egress quarterly. Anything in egress but not in the inventory is either an addition or a remediation. Use Phin, Hatching, or just SIEM correlations against a curated AI-domain list.

aws_bedrock.summary: AWS Config conformance packs against Bedrock and SageMaker resources reconcile the inventory automatically. Drift becomes a Security Hub finding.

azure_foundry.summary: Azure Policy compliance state over the AI resource types reconciles the declared inventory against what exists. Defender for Cloud AI posture surfaces deployments nobody registered.

links.label: Defender for Cloud AI security posture

google_vertex_ai.summary: Security Command Center asset inventory is the reconciliation source. Anything present but unregistered is either an addition to the inventory or a removal from the estate.

title: Basic understanding of AI risks at the leadership level
summary: Leadership recognizes AI as a risk category but does not yet have a defended risk taxonomy or assigned risk owners.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Adopt a five-risk taxonomy and stop there for now: data leakage, model misuse, third-party AI, regulatory, hallucination/legal. Anything more granular is overkill at Stage 2.

title: No AI-specific security testing
summary: Existing pentests do not include prompt injection, model extraction, or instruction-manipulation cases. AI components are in scope only by accident.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Add an AI testing rider to the next pentest scope. At minimum: prompt injection (direct and indirect), output handling for PII, and basic model extraction prompts. Garak and Promptfoo cover most of this in OSS.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock model evaluation supports automated and human evaluation jobs against curated test sets, including custom adversarial sets seeded by Garak or Promptfoo output.

azure_foundry.summary: The AI Red Teaming agent runs automated adversarial scans against a deployed endpoint, and the risk and safety evaluators score the results across a fixed set of harm categories, so results are comparable run to run.

google_vertex_ai.summary: The gen AI evaluation service runs curated and custom adversarial sets against a deployed model. Model Armor's screening results give a second signal on prompt injection and jailbreak attempts in production traffic.

title: Basic visibility into where models originate
summary: Engineering can describe where the models in use came from (vendor, Hugging Face org, internal build), but provenance is not verified cryptographically or tracked in a registry.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Adopt an internal model registry (MLflow, ZenML, or a folder in object storage with hashes and a README). Record source URL, hash, license, and approver.

aws_bedrock.summary: JumpStart model cards and Marketplace listing pages record source, license, training data attestation, and version. Pin to model ARNs in code rather than friendly names.

azure_foundry.summary: The Foundry catalog records publisher, license, and version; the Azure ML registry does the same for anything you build. Pin deployments to a registered version rather than a floating alias.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Model Registry versions every model with its source and lineage. Reference the version resource name in code, not the display name.

title: Awareness that pickled model files pose risk
summary: Engineers know pickle deserialization is dangerous but verification is ad hoc.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Mandate safetensors for new internal artifacts. Quarantine any pickle that has not been scanned by ModelScan or picklescan.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock foundation models do not load customer-supplied pickle artifacts. For SageMaker custom training, restrict input sources to S3 buckets owned by the workload account and pickle-scan as part of the data pipeline.

azure_foundry.summary: Managed Foundry models do not load customer-supplied pickle artifacts. For Azure ML custom training, restrict inputs to workspace-owned datastores and scan artifacts in the pipeline before registration.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Managed endpoints do not load customer pickle files. For custom training, keep inputs in project-owned buckets inside the VPC Service Controls perimeter and make the scan a pipeline step.

title: Basic awareness of the risks of granting AI tools API access or system integrations
summary: The organization knows that granting a chatbot or assistant API tokens carries risk, but there is no review process before grants are issued.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Require a short threat-model exercise on any AI tool that requests scopes broader than read-only. Add the integration to the asset register before any grant is approved.

aws_bedrock.summary: Treat any AWS principal granted `bedrock-agent:*`, `lambda:InvokeFunction` across boundaries, or cross-account assume-role into an AI workload as an agentic integration requiring threat-model review.

azure_foundry.summary: Any managed identity granted an Agent Service role, or any connection to an external tool, is an agentic integration. Review the role assignment before the connection is created, not after.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Any service account bound to an agent deployment or a tool connector is an agentic integration. Review the IAM binding, not just the application design.

title: Security tools with AI-based features used but not intentionally configured
summary: AI features in the SIEM/EDR are turned on but no one has tuned thresholds, evaluated detections against environment data, or measured false-positive rates.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Pick one AI feature per tool. Document baseline false-positive rate over a fixed window. Tune. Repeat.

aws_bedrock.summary: GuardDuty, Inspector, and Security Hub all ship measurable detection sets. Tune each in a documented sequence, measuring suppression vs. additional findings against a labeled month of incident data.

azure_foundry.summary: Defender for Cloud AI threat protection and Sentinel analytics both expose per-rule tuning. Baseline for a month, tune, and record what changed and why.

links.label: Defender for Cloud AI threat protection

google_vertex_ai.summary: Security Command Center detectors and SecOps rules both support per-rule tuning and muting. Measure the false-positive rate before and after each change.

title: No customization or tuning of AI security features
summary: Detections, summarizations, and alert classifications all run at vendor defaults regardless of environment fit.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Allocate analyst time for tuning. Vendor defaults assume a generic environment; an unconfigured AI feature is usually noisier than its predecessor rule-based detection.

title: Basic spam/malware detection using vendor AI
summary: Mail and endpoint vendors apply their own AI models to detection, but the organization does not contribute telemetry back or evaluate the outcome.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Capture monthly detection rates from each vendor with AI-backed detection. Build a single internal dashboard that compares.

aws_bedrock.summary: GuardDuty Malware Protection plus Amazon SES email feedback metrics give a measurable baseline. Pipe both into a single Security Hub dashboard.

azure_foundry.summary: The Defender products report their own detection rates per workload. Surface them in one Sentinel workbook rather than reading three vendor consoles separately.

title: No AI strategy for security operations
summary: There is no roadmap for where AI augmentation should land in the SOC workflow.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Pick one workflow (alert triage, IR write-up generation, threat intel summarization) and target it for Stage 3 enablement. Do not try to AI-augment the whole SOC at once.

aws_bedrock.summary: Security Hub's posture management gives a coverage map to plan against. Pick one workflow and target a Bedrock-backed automation (alert summarization or playbook explanation) as the first integration.

azure_foundry.summary: Pick one workflow and target Foundry-backed automation for it. Sentinel automation rules are the integration point; Foundry observability supplies the evaluation data to judge whether it worked.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Pick one workflow and drive it from a SecOps playbook that calls a model. The gen AI evaluation service gives the before-and-after measure.

title: Security team lacks AI/ML skills
summary: No team member has hands-on experience with prompt engineering, model evaluation, or ML pipeline security.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Send at least one engineer through SANS SEC545 or equivalent. Cross-train so AI security knowledge does not concentrate in a single person.

links.label: SANS SEC545: GenAI and LLM Application Security

title: No validation of vendor AI claims
summary: Vendors marketing 'AI-powered' features are accepted at face value. There is no test against environment data or measured outcome.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Add a short AI questionnaire to vendor reviews: what model, on whose data, with what evaluation, under what retention. Refuse procurement of 'AI' features that cannot answer.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock Marketplace and JumpStart listings include the model card, license, and benchmark scores when available. Treat that as the bar for any AI vendor: if they cannot match Marketplace metadata, refuse procurement.

azure_foundry.summary: Foundry catalog entries carry the model card, license, and evaluation metadata. Treat that as the minimum any procured AI feature must be able to answer.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Model Garden listings carry the model card and license. Ask a vendor the same three questions: which model, trained on whose data, evaluated how.

title: AI acceptable use policy published; may be binary rather than nuanced
summary: An AUP exists. Common shape: a list of allowed tools, a list of prohibited tools, and a paragraph on data classes.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Annual policy review with a feedback channel. The Stage 2 policy will be wrong; the only way to improve it is to make it easy to challenge.

aws_bedrock.summary: Encode the policy in SCPs and IAM tag-based conditions. The policy text is the human-readable layer; the SCP is the enforcement layer that prevents drift between intent and reality.

azure_foundry.summary: Azure Policy definitions assigned at the management group are the enforcement layer beneath the policy text: allowed regions, allowed model deployments, required diagnostic settings.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Organization policy constraints are the enforcement layer: which services, which regions, which projects. The policy document is the readable version of the same rules.

title: Data classification for AI usage is absent or incomplete
summary: The AUP references data classes but the underlying data classification work has not been done or is partial.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Data classification is the Stage 3 prerequisite. If it is not done, this is the next thing to fund. Use Presidio for PII detection in unstructured stores.

aws_bedrock.summary: Macie auto-classifies S3 objects against managed and custom data identifiers. Run a one-shot scan over the data lake to surface PHI / PII / financial data before drafting the AI data classification rules.

azure_foundry.summary: Purview classifies and labels the data estate; DSPM for AI then reports which classified data is actually reaching AI tools, which is the number the policy needs.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Sensitive Data Protection scans and classifies the estate, and Dataplex carries the catalog and governance metadata that the AI data rules reference.

title: Basic awareness training mentions AI risks
summary: AI is referenced in annual security training but not addressed in role-specific depth.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Add a five-minute module: what to never paste into AI tools, what to do if you find an AI feature in a vendor product, where to report.

title: No AI risk register
summary: AI risks are not tracked alongside other enterprise risks with owners, treatments, and review cadence.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Add an 'AI' risk category to the existing enterprise risk register. Three to five risks at this stage. Owner, current treatment, residual rating, review date.

aws_bedrock.summary: Use AWS Audit Manager's Generative AI Best Practices framework as the seed for the register; its assessments map to common control families (CC, AC, AT) and emit evidence artifacts.

azure_foundry.summary: Run the Well-Architected AI workload assessment and seed the register from its gap list, so the first entries are specific rather than generic.

google_vertex_ai.summary: The Architecture Framework security pillar plus current Security Command Center posture findings seed the register with gaps that are already true in the estate.

title: No cross-functional AI governance body
summary: AI decisions are made in silos: legal in one channel, engineering in another, security in a third.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Form a working group, not a committee. Standing 30-minute monthly meeting, named members from security, legal, engineering, and a business sponsor. Output is a public decisions log.

title: Policy begins to differentiate between conversational AI and AI granted permission to take actions
summary: The AUP distinguishes chat-style AI from agentic AI in scope and review requirements.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Define 'agentic AI' in the policy: any AI that invokes tools, writes to systems, or sends communications. Require a security architecture review before any agentic deployment.

aws_bedrock.summary: In AWS terms: `bedrock:InvokeModel` is conversational, `bedrock-agent:*` and AgentCore are agentic. Write the policy with these IAM action families as the dividing line so enforcement is structural, not narrative.

azure_foundry.summary: Draw the line at the Agent Service: inference role assignments are conversational, Agent Service and connection roles are agentic. The role assignment is then the auditable boundary.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Draw the line at the agent runtime: model inference permissions are conversational, agent deployment and tool bindings are agentic.

title: Complete inventory of AI systems and models; AI included in asset classification
summary: Every AI system, model, agent, and AI-augmented SaaS feature is recorded with owner, classification, approved use, and review cadence.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Promote the asset register to a system of record with API access for SIEM/SOAR. Reconcile automatically against egress logs and IdP grants.

aws_bedrock.summary: AWS Config recorder for Bedrock, SageMaker, and Lambda resources, with custom rules for AI-specific attributes (model used, knowledge base attached, agent role). Findings to Security Hub.

azure_foundry.summary: Azure Policy compliance state over the AI resource types is the automated reconciliation, and Defender for Cloud AI posture surfaces deployments that exist but were never registered. Export both on a schedule instead of hand-maintaining the register.

links.label: Defender for Cloud AI security posture

google_vertex_ai.summary: Security Command Center asset inventory is the authoritative resource list and organization policy bounds where resources can appear at all. Export assets and findings on a schedule into the register.

title: Data flows to and from AI systems are documented with data lineage visibility
summary: For each AI system, the data classes consumed, generated, and persisted are documented end to end.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Use OpenLineage or a comparable lineage tool for ETL into model contexts. Capture system prompt, tool definitions, retrieval index, and output sink.

aws_bedrock.summary: Use AWS DataZone or a SageMaker Feature Store catalog for upstream data lineage. For Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the data source manifest plus CloudTrail data events give end-to-end retrieval lineage.

azure_foundry.summary: Purview holds the upstream data map. On the Foundry side, the project's connections and the index behind a retrieval flow define what the model can read, and DSPM for AI reports which classified data actually reaches a prompt.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Dataplex carries the upstream catalog and lineage, ML metadata records dataset-to-model lineage inside the platform, and the grounding configuration documents what a model can retrieve at inference time.

title: Internal AI agents assigned distinct NHIs with strict access control
summary: Every AI agent has its own Non-Human Identity with scoped credentials, a documented human owner, and least-privilege access to tools, data, and APIs.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Issue short-lived credentials per agent via Vault or SPIFFE. Scope each agent to a single tool surface. Every credential ties back to a named human owner in the asset register.

aws_bedrock.summary: AgentCore Identity issues per-agent IAM roles scoped to `bedrock:InvokeModel` on specific model ARNs and to the exact tool ARNs each agent needs. Tie the role tag to a human-owner attribute enforced by SCP.

azure_foundry.summary: Give every agent its own user-assigned managed identity rather than sharing one. Scope the Foundry role assignment to the specific project and connections that agent needs, and keep any non-Entra secret in Key Vault with that identity as the only reader.

google_vertex_ai.summary: One service account per agent, bound only to the model and tool resources it needs. Use workload identity federation for anything running outside the project so no service account key is ever exported.

title: AI tool and API access strictly scoped
summary: AI tool access is scoped to specific resources, time windows, and operations. No broad credentials.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Define a tool-access policy DSL (OPA, Cedar) that scopes per-agent invocations. Deny by default; allow per tool, per resource.

aws_bedrock.summary: IAM condition keys (`aws:RequestTag`, `bedrock:ModelId`, `bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier`) narrow Invoke permissions to specific models, with guardrails, and for tagged callers.

azure_foundry.summary: Scope role assignments to the individual project and deployment rather than the subscription, and put Conditional Access on the calling identity. Access is then bounded by resource, caller, and network location at once.

google_vertex_ai.summary: IAM conditions on the model and endpoint resources bound access per caller; a VPC Service Controls perimeter bounds it per network path. Deny by default at the project level with organization policy.

title: Prompt injection and instruction manipulation defenses implemented
summary: Production AI systems apply layered defenses: input segregation, instruction hierarchy, retrieval sanitization, and output validation.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Combine LLM Guard or NeMo Guardrails for I/O filtering with a system-prompt design that places untrusted content in a clearly demarcated section. Test with Garak and Promptfoo in CI.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock Guardrails apply content filtering, denied topics, contextual grounding checks, and PII redaction inline at InvokeModel time. Combine with prompt-template hygiene that segregates retrieval context.

azure_foundry.summary: Prompt Shields screens for direct jailbreak and for indirect injection embedded in retrieved documents, and the content filter runs inline on both prompt and completion. Add groundedness detection wherever the application is retrieval-backed.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Model Armor screens prompts and responses for injection and jailbreak independently of the model, so the control does not have to move when the model does. Safety filters cover the harm categories and grounding bounds what retrieval can inject.

title: Input validation and output filtering deployed
summary: User-facing AI applications validate inputs against schema and filter outputs for PII, sensitive markers, and unsafe content.

cloud_agnostic.summary: LLM Guard or Promptfoo's redactor for outputs. Presidio for PII. Block-on-confidence rather than allow-on-pass.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock Guardrails for inline filtering, plus Macie scanning of any data the model has read or written to S3. PII redaction settings on the guardrail are scoped per use case.

azure_foundry.summary: The content filter runs on input and output with per-category severity thresholds, and custom categories cover organization-specific terms the stock categories miss. Purview DLP catches classified data on the way in.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Model Armor sanitizes both prompt and response, using Sensitive Data Protection inspection templates to define which data classes get redacted rather than hand-listing patterns.

title: AI systems included in penetration testing scope; basic adversarial emulation conducted
summary: AI systems are scoped into routine pentests with named adversarial test cases.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Add ATLAS-aligned test cases to the pentest SOW. Require evidence of prompt-injection, model-extraction, and instruction-manipulation attempts in the report.

aws_bedrock.summary: AWS customer support policy allows testing of customer-owned AI workloads on Bedrock without prior approval; bring the ATLAS-aligned test cases and supply prompt-injection seeds. Bedrock Guardrails will return blocked-content metadata that helps measure defense efficacy.

azure_foundry.summary: Run the AI Red Teaming agent as part of the engagement rather than only ad hoc. It produces a scored, repeatable report per harm category that the pentest can build on and that later runs can be compared against.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Use the gen AI evaluation service against adversarial sets as the repeatable baseline, and treat Model Armor's blocked-request telemetry as the efficacy measure for the defense rather than a finding count.

title: Model provenance verification in place
summary: Every model entering the environment is verified against its publisher signature or hash before deployment.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Mirror approved models internally with signed manifests. Sigstore for signing. Block direct download from external registries at the egress proxy.

aws_bedrock.summary: JumpStart and Bedrock Marketplace models are signed by AWS or the model publisher and pinned by ARN. Custom models trained via SageMaker can be registered with model approval status and lineage in the registry.

azure_foundry.summary: Catalogued models are published by Microsoft or by the model publisher and are pinned by deployment. For self-built models, register in the Azure ML registry so version, lineage, and approval state exist before anything is deployed.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Model Garden entries carry publisher and license; Model Registry records version and lineage for anything you build. Binary Authorization enforces that only attested container images can serve.

title: Controls mapped to MITRE ATLAS techniques
summary: Defensive controls are inventoried and mapped to the ATLAS techniques they address, exposing coverage gaps.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Reuse the same MITRE ATT&CK Navigator approach you already use for endpoint coverage. ATLAS Navigator JSON is published.

title: Runtime validation of dynamically loaded agent tools and plugins
summary: Agent tool definitions, descriptions, and capabilities are validated at load time against an allow-list of approved tool signatures.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Hash each registered tool definition. Refuse to load a tool whose signature has changed since approval. Audit changes through code review, not at run time.

azure_foundry.summary: Agent Service tools and connections are declared resources, so a change to one is an ARM operation in the activity log. Deploy them from templates and treat any out-of-band change as drift to investigate.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Agent tool bindings are resource and IAM changes, which land in audit logs. Deploy them declaratively and alert on any tool binding that changes outside the pipeline.

title: Secure agent-to-agent communication and mutual authentication
summary: Agents authenticate to each other with mTLS or workload identity; messages are bound to identities, not trust-by-default channels.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Service mesh with mTLS (Linkerd, Istio) or SPIFFE SVIDs for direct agent-to-agent calls. Apply OPA policy at the receiving side.

aws_bedrock.summary: Use AgentCore for managed inter-agent communication. For self-hosted agents on ECS or EKS, App Mesh or VPC Lattice with TLS plus IAM auth provides equivalent mutual authentication.

azure_foundry.summary: Put the Agent Service in a managed virtual network with private endpoints so inter-agent traffic never leaves the perimeter, and authenticate with managed identities rather than shared keys.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Bind each agent to its own service account and keep calls inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter, so identity comes from IAM rather than from network position.

title: AI-powered threat detection tuned to the environment
summary: AI-based detections are tuned against organizational data, with measured precision and recall.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Tune each detection against historical incident data. Capture precision/recall on a labeled subset before promoting a detection to production.

aws_bedrock.summary: GuardDuty and Security Hub provide tunable detection thresholds. SageMaker custom models trained on local detection data integrate via Lambda detectors that emit Security Hub findings.

azure_foundry.summary: Sentinel analytics rules and Defender for Cloud AI alerts are the tunable surface. Score each against historical incident data and record the precision measure with the rule before promoting it.

links.label: Defender for Cloud AI threat protection

google_vertex_ai.summary: Tune Security Command Center detectors and SecOps rules against historical incident data, and keep the measured precision alongside the rule so later changes are comparable.

title: AI-assisted alert triage and prioritization in place
summary: An AI layer triages incoming alerts: deduplication, severity ranking, and recommended next action.

cloud_agnostic.summary: If vendor SOAR ships AI triage, enable and measure it. Where it does not, a small LLM front-end against alert payloads (with redaction) can do the same job for routine alert classes.

aws_bedrock.summary: Lambda-based alert summarization using Bedrock InvokeModel with a guardrail that redacts PII before model invocation. Output back into Security Hub as a note.

azure_foundry.summary: A Logic App calling a Foundry deployment does the summarization, with the content filter inline and a Purview DLP redaction step ahead of the call. Sentinel holds the result as an incident comment.

google_vertex_ai.summary: A SecOps playbook calls the model with Model Armor in front of it. Run Sensitive Data Protection over the alert payload before the call rather than trusting the prompt to withhold it.

title: Behavioral analytics (UEBA) deployed and customized for anomaly detection
summary: UEBA models cover users, service accounts, and AI agent NHIs.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Extend UEBA models to include AI agent NHIs as a distinct identity class with their own baselines.

aws_bedrock.summary: GuardDuty IAM finding types behave as UEBA for AWS principals. Add a custom detection layer for Bedrock invocation patterns: model, region, prompt-size distributions per IAM role.

azure_foundry.summary: Sentinel UEBA baselines users and service principals. Add the agent managed identities as their own entity class so agent behavior is not averaged into the human baseline.

google_vertex_ai.summary: SecOps behavioral analytics covers principals. Add agent service accounts as a distinct entity class and baseline invocation patterns per model and per region.

title: AI-assisted automated playbooks deployed for common scenarios
summary: Routine response actions (phishing reports, suspect IP triage) are partially or fully automated with AI assistance.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Adopt or extend an OSS SOAR (Shuffle, TheHive Cortex). Pair AI summarization with deterministic action steps; never let an LLM be the sole decider on a containment action at this stage.

aws_bedrock.summary: Step Functions orchestrates the deterministic steps; Bedrock InvokeModel as a Lambda task handles the language work (write-ups, classification). Never let Bedrock be the sole decider on a containment branch.

azure_foundry.summary: Sentinel automation rules trigger Logic Apps for the deterministic steps and call a Foundry deployment only for the language work. Containment stays on a deterministic branch.

google_vertex_ai.summary: SecOps playbooks run the deterministic steps and call a model only for summarization and classification. Containment stays on a deterministic branch.

title: AI-powered threat intelligence enrichment
summary: Incoming threat intel is automatically enriched (entity extraction, related-actor mapping, summarization).

cloud_agnostic.summary: Run intel through an LLM with extraction prompts (entities, TTPs, IOCs) and post structured output back into the TIP.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock with a structured-output guardrail for entity / TTP / IOC extraction. Inferentia or Trainium instances handle high-volume enrichment more cost-effectively than on-demand model pricing.

azure_foundry.summary: A Foundry deployment with structured-output prompting handles entity, TTP, and IOC extraction; Sentinel's threat intelligence tables are the sink. Batch the calls rather than invoking per indicator.

google_vertex_ai.summary: A batched model call with structured output handles extraction, and SecOps holds the enriched intel. Batching matters here: per-indicator invocation is the usual cost surprise.

title: Security team trained on AI/ML fundamentals
summary: Engineers understand model evaluation basics, prompt engineering, and AI failure modes.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Adopt a role-based training matrix: general workforce (15 min), engineers (2 hours), AI specialists (multi-day).

aws_bedrock.summary: AWS Skill Builder ML and security learning plans plus the AWS Generative AI Security Scoping Matrix as the org-internal reference. Annual recertification on the matrix.

azure_foundry.summary: Microsoft's AI Red Team guidance and the Well-Architected AI workload content make a usable internal reference set for the engineer tier of the training matrix.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Google's Secure AI Framework and the Architecture Framework security pillar make the equivalent internal reference set for the engineer tier.

title: Genuine AI/ML capability and environment compatibility assessed at procurement
summary: Vendors selling AI features must demonstrate genuine capability and fit; AI-washing is rejected.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Require model cards, adversarial test results, and a defined evaluation set from any AI vendor. No proof, no procurement.

aws_bedrock.summary: Marketplace and JumpStart listings include model cards; treat their structure as the bar for non-AWS vendors. No model card, no procurement.

azure_foundry.summary: Catalogued models publish a model card and the safety evaluation methodology is documented. A vendor that cannot produce the equivalent has not demonstrated capability.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Model Garden listings publish the model card, and the evaluation service defines what a defensible evaluation looks like. Ask vendors for both artifacts.

title: AI Governance Council established with cross-functional membership and decision authority
summary: A standing body with security, legal, privacy, engineering, and business representation makes binding decisions on AI use cases.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Publish the charter. Publish decisions. Republish quarterly.

title: Comprehensive AI policy addressing use cases and data classification
summary: Policy is specific by use case and by data class, not binary block/allow.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Map approved tools to data classes in a single table. The policy reads in seconds.

aws_bedrock.summary: Map the policy table to IAM permission boundaries and tag-condition policies; the human-readable policy and the SCP set should be reconciled monthly.

azure_foundry.summary: Reconcile the policy table against Azure Policy assignments and role definitions monthly. The readable table and the enforced rules drift apart quietly otherwise.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Reconcile the policy table against organization policy constraints and IAM role bindings monthly, in the same review.

title: AI ethics guidelines established
summary: Ethical considerations (fairness, transparency, human oversight) are codified.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Use NIST AI RMF Playbook prompts to seed the ethics guidelines rather than writing from scratch.

azure_foundry.summary: The Azure OpenAI transparency note documents intended uses, limitations, and known failure modes per model, which is the concrete input the ethics guidelines need. The Responsible AI dashboard covers fairness and error analysis for models you train.

google_vertex_ai.summary: The platform's responsible AI documentation covers the same ground: intended use, limitations, and the safety attributes the models are filtered against.

title: Third-party AI assessment requirements defined
summary: Vendor AI systems are assessed against a defined questionnaire before purchase.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Adopt a standard vendor AI questionnaire (HiTRUST AI Risk Management, NIST AI 100-1 derived). Refuse to onboard vendors that decline.

aws_bedrock.summary: Marketplace vendor profiles publish model cards, eval results, and provenance. Build the in-house questionnaire to mirror Marketplace metadata so internal evaluation aligns with the canonical source.

azure_foundry.summary: The transparency note and catalog metadata define what a complete vendor answer looks like on capability, limitation, and data handling. Build the questionnaire to ask for the same fields.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Ask vendors the retention question explicitly: the platform documents zero data retention terms per model, which gives you a concrete standard to hold third parties to.

title: AI risks included in the enterprise risk register with a defined assessment methodology
summary: AI risks use a documented method (likelihood, impact, treatment) consistent with the rest of the register.

cloud_agnostic.summary: FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk) extended for AI scenarios is the most common starting point at Stage 3 to 4.

aws_bedrock.summary: Audit Manager assessments emit structured evidence that feeds a FAIR-extended methodology cleanly. Use the Generative AI framework as the starting assessment set and add custom controls per AI scenario.

azure_foundry.summary: Defender for Cloud AI posture findings supply the exposure side of the likelihood estimate with current data, so the register is scored against the estate as it is rather than as documented.

links.label: Defender for Cloud AI security posture

google_vertex_ai.summary: Security Command Center posture and vulnerability findings supply the current exposure data behind the likelihood estimate.

title: AI-specific incident response procedures in place
summary: IR playbooks address prompt injection, model exfiltration, agent misuse, and AI vendor outages.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Add 'AI incident' as a category in the IR runbook with sub-types: prompt injection, agent misuse, data exfiltration via output, model unavailability.

aws_bedrock.summary: Add Bedrock-specific runbooks: prompt-injection containment (rotate the guardrail and the agent role), data exfiltration via output (revoke Bedrock invoke for the offending role, capture invocation logs for the window), agent misuse (decommission the AgentCore identity).

azure_foundry.summary: Write Foundry-specific runbooks: on injection, tighten the content filter policy and rotate the agent identity; on output-based exfiltration, remove the role assignment and pull invocation logs for the window; on agent misuse, delete the managed identity. Sentinel holds the case.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Write platform-specific runbooks: on injection, update the Model Armor template and rotate the agent service account; on exfiltration, remove the IAM binding and pull Data Access logs for the window; on agent misuse, delete the service account.

title: Human-in-the-loop thresholds and automated policy enforcement defined for high-risk agent workflows
summary: Policy decision points, intent gates, and consequence-based checks are defined for high-risk agentic actions.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Codify a 'consequence ladder': low-impact actions can run autonomously, mid-impact require log review, high-impact require synchronous human approval.

aws_bedrock.summary: Step Functions has a wait-for-human-task pattern; AgentCore supports action policies that require explicit approval. Define the consequence ladder once and reference it from both.

azure_foundry.summary: Keep the consequence ladder in one document and reference it from both the agent's tool configuration and the Logic App that carries the approval step, so the two cannot disagree.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Keep the consequence ladder in one document and enforce it in both the agent's tool configuration and the workflow that carries the approval step.

title: Every deployed AI agent has a documented human owner
summary: No anonymous agents; every running agent ties to a named human.

cloud_agnostic.summary: The asset register's 'owner' column is the source of truth. Any agent without an owner is decommissioned.

aws_bedrock.summary: Enforce a required tag (Owner=<human-IAM-Identity-Center-user>) on every AgentCore identity via SCP. AWS Config rule flags identities missing the tag for decommission.

azure_foundry.summary: Require an Owner tag on every agent identity and Foundry project and enforce it with an Azure Policy deny effect, so an untagged resource cannot be created in the first place.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Require an owner label on every agent service account and deployment, enforced with organization policy and checked by a Security Command Center posture rule.

title: Structured logging with trace IDs across agent steps and tool calls
summary: Every agent action carries a trace ID that links back to the originating request, system prompt, tool invocation, and result.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, or OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions cover this.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock model invocation logging captures request, response, and guardrail decision; AgentCore traces capture each tool step. Stream both to CloudWatch Logs with a per-trace correlation ID; export to S3 for long retention.

azure_foundry.summary: Foundry observability emits OpenTelemetry traces per agent run including each tool step. Route them to a Log Analytics workspace and carry a correlation ID so a single request can be reconstructed end to end.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Cloud Audit Logs record each invocation and the agent runtime emits per-step traces. Carry one correlation ID across both and export to a long-retention sink.

title: Security integrated into the AI/ML development lifecycle
summary: Security gates exist at each phase of the AI lifecycle: design, data, training, eval, deploy, monitor.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Define gate criteria per phase. Tie to the standard SDLC change-management workflow.

aws_bedrock.summary: SageMaker Pipelines with Model Cards, Model Monitor, and Clarify covers the end-to-end lifecycle. Promote each pipeline stage to a Security Hub control so gate evidence is centralized.

azure_foundry.summary: Azure ML pipelines carry the gates: data validation, evaluation, and registration are pipeline steps with recorded outputs, and registration is what deployment reads from. Foundry evaluations run as a gate before a deployment is promoted.

google_vertex_ai.summary: ML pipelines carry the gate steps and write lineage into ML metadata, so gate evidence is attached to the model version rather than living in a build log.

title: Threat modeling required for all AI systems
summary: STRIDE or PASTA threat models extended for AI threats are mandatory before deployment.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Use the OWASP AI Exchange threat tree as the AI-specific extension to whatever threat-modeling method the org already uses.

title: Confused Deputy defenses deployed to isolate untrusted inputs from agent execution tools
summary: An agent's authority to invoke tools is bound to the request context, not the agent itself, preventing untrusted user inputs from inducing high-authority actions.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Use OPA or Cedar at the tool boundary with the request principal in the policy, not just the agent identity.

aws_bedrock.summary: Add a Lambda authorizer to the AgentCore tool path that re-evaluates the request principal, not just the agent role. AgentCore action policies can carry the consequence ladder as policy attributes.

azure_foundry.summary: Put an authorization step in front of the tool that evaluates the calling user's identity, not just the agent's managed identity. Foundry role assignments bound what the agent could ever do; the request-time check bounds what it may do now.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Evaluate the end user's identity at the tool boundary rather than relying on the agent's service account. IAM conditions bound the agent's ceiling; the request-time check binds authority to the request.

title: Execution guardrails with real-time monitoring for AI agent API calls
summary: Each agent API call is evaluated in real time against the agent's scope and the current consequence ladder.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Combine NeMo Guardrails for I/O with a policy engine (OPA/Cedar) for action authorization. Log denies for tuning.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock Guardrails (content filters, denied topics, contextual grounding) plus AgentCore action policies. Pair with a Lambda authorizer in the tool path that re-evaluates the request principal and consequence rating.

azure_foundry.summary: The content filter and Prompt Shields evaluate every call inline, and Foundry observability records the decision per run so denies are tunable rather than invisible.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Model Armor evaluates every prompt and response against the template, and its findings are the tuning signal. Keep the authorization decision separate from the content decision.

title: Comprehensive AI model and agentic red teaming program
summary: A dedicated AI red team conducts continuous adversarial assessments distinct from traditional pentesting.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Stand up a recurring red-team cadence with documented test plans. AI red teaming is distinct from pentesting (which exercises the surrounding application).

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock model evaluation supports custom adversarial test sets. Pipe Garak and Promptfoo outputs into evaluation jobs and track findings as Security Hub items.

azure_foundry.summary: The AI Red Teaming agent supports scheduled scans with custom attack objectives, so the red-team cadence produces comparable scores instead of one-off reports.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Run the evaluation service against maintained adversarial sets on a cadence, and version the sets alongside the model so a regression is attributable.

title: Controls for cascading failures in multi-agent systems
summary: When one agent fails or is compromised, isolation prevents propagation through shared memory, delegated tasks, or trusted communication channels.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Partition shared memory per agent. Treat agent-to-agent messages as untrusted input and apply the same I/O guardrails as external input.

aws_bedrock.summary: Per-agent SQS queues with DLQs prevent message propagation on failure. Bedrock Guardrails can be agent-specific so a compromise of one agent does not lower the policy bar of another.

azure_foundry.summary: Give each agent its own identity and its own connections so a compromise cannot borrow another agent's reach, and keep agent-to-agent traffic inside the managed virtual network where it can be observed.

google_vertex_ai.summary: One service account and one perimeter-scoped set of resources per agent. Treat inter-agent messages as untrusted input and run them through the same screening as external input.

title: Automated adversarial testing integrated into CI/CD pipelines
summary: Every AI build is tested against an adversarial suite before deployment.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Add Garak and Promptfoo runs to CI. Fail builds on regression beyond a defined tolerance.

aws_bedrock.summary: CodePipeline stage that runs Bedrock evaluation against the build candidate. Fail the stage on regression beyond tolerance.

azure_foundry.summary: Run the red teaming agent and the risk and safety evaluators as a pipeline step against the build candidate, and fail the build on regression beyond a defined tolerance.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Run the evaluation service as a pipeline step against the build candidate; the pipeline records the score against the model version so regressions are traceable.

title: MITRE ATLAS alignment covering the full kill chain
summary: Controls are mapped to ATLAS techniques across all tactics including exfiltration and impact.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Use the ATLAS Navigator with explicit coverage tracking; gaps drive next quarter's roadmap.

title: Automated model scanning and provenance verification
summary: Every model artifact is scanned for known-bad serialization, malicious operators, and signature mismatches.

cloud_agnostic.summary: ModelScan + safetensors-only enforcement in CI for first-party models; signed manifests for third-party.

aws_bedrock.summary: Inspector scans container images that host inference workloads. For raw model artifacts, run ModelScan in a build step and publish the result to Security Hub.

azure_foundry.summary: Scan the serving container images and register only scanned artifacts. Deployment reads from the registry, so an unscanned artifact has no path to production.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Artifact Analysis scans the serving images and Binary Authorization refuses to deploy anything without a passing attestation, which makes the scan a gate rather than a report.

title: Real-time prompt injection detection
summary: Inline detection of prompt-injection patterns, instruction inversion, and known jailbreak signatures.

cloud_agnostic.summary: LLM Guard inline. Custom detectors for environment-specific patterns.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock Guardrails apply prompt-injection-aware content filters in line at invoke time. Pair with a Guardrails CloudWatch metric alarm for blocked-content trending.

azure_foundry.summary: Prompt Shields runs inline on every call, covering direct jailbreak and indirect injection in retrieved content. Alert on the blocked-request rate rather than reading the log.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Model Armor screens each prompt and response inline. Send its findings to Security Command Center so blocked-request trends surface with the rest of the security signal.

title: MLSecOps implemented: secure pipelines, model versioning and provenance, training data validation
summary: An end-to-end MLSecOps pipeline covers data, training, eval, deploy, and monitoring with security gates at each step.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Treat ML pipelines as software supply-chain risks: signed artifacts, dataset provenance, reproducible training, evaluation gates.

aws_bedrock.summary: SageMaker Pipelines with Model Cards, Model Monitor, Clarify (bias and explainability), and the Model Registry. Provenance and approval gating native; integrate with EventBridge to feed Security Hub on policy violation.

azure_foundry.summary: Azure ML pipelines cover data, training, evaluation, and registration with model monitoring after deployment. The Responsible AI dashboard supplies the evaluation artifacts the gates check.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Pipelines cover the lifecycle, ML metadata records the lineage, and model monitoring closes the loop after deployment. Binary Authorization gates what can actually serve.

title: Custom ML models developed for organization-specific threat detection
summary: Internal models trained on local data outperform generic vendor models in measured ways.

cloud_agnostic.summary: MLflow or ZenML for training pipelines. Capture training data lineage, eval set, and deployment metadata.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock Custom Models for foundation model fine-tunes, SageMaker for from-scratch training. Both write into the SageMaker Model Registry with lineage and approval status.

azure_foundry.summary: Azure ML handles training with experiment tracking; the registry records lineage and approval state. Evaluate against the same held-out set each time so 'outperforms the generic model' is a measured claim.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Train through pipelines with experiment tracking, register versions in Model Registry, and keep the evaluation set versioned alongside so improvement is measurable rather than asserted.

title: AI-powered deception technologies and honeypots deployed
summary: Honeypots and decoy assets are generated and managed with AI assistance.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Generate realistic decoy documents, accounts, and endpoints with LLM assistance. Watch for any access.

title: Autonomous response enabled for defined, validated scenarios
summary: Specific response actions run without human approval when triggered by validated, high-confidence detections.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Maintain a whitelist of autonomous actions, with measured false-positive ceilings. Anything outside the whitelist still requires human approval.

aws_bedrock.summary: Step Functions state machines call AWS APIs autonomously for whitelisted actions; AgentCore for the same with stricter audit. CloudWatch Synthetics for measured FP rate prior to whitelist expansion.

azure_foundry.summary: Keep the autonomous action list in the Sentinel automation rule itself, so the whitelist and the enforcement are the same object. Measure the false-positive rate of the triggering rule before expanding it.

links.label: Defender for Cloud AI threat protection

google_vertex_ai.summary: Keep the autonomous action list in the SecOps playbook, and measure the triggering detector's false-positive rate before adding an action to it.

title: SOAR platform enhanced with AI-driven decision support
summary: SOAR playbooks consume AI-driven recommendations at branch points.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Capture AI recommendations alongside human decisions. Audit divergence to tune.

aws_bedrock.summary: Step Functions and Lambda for orchestration; Bedrock for recommendation generation; Security Hub for routing and metric capture. Capture human override vs. AI recommendation as a tuning signal.

azure_foundry.summary: Sentinel automation rules carry the playbook and a Foundry deployment supplies the recommendation at branch points. Record the recommendation and the human decision on the incident so divergence is measurable.

google_vertex_ai.summary: SecOps playbooks carry the branch logic and a model call supplies the recommendation. Record recommendation and human decision together so divergence can be tuned against.

title: AI-powered threat hunting operational
summary: Hunt hypotheses generated by AI agents and validated by humans.

cloud_agnostic.summary: LLM front-ends against SIEM data for hypothesis generation. Hunt outcomes feed detection authoring.

aws_bedrock.summary: Athena over Security Lake or CloudTrail data for hypothesis generation with Bedrock; resulting detections promoted to GuardDuty custom threat lists or SIEM rules.

azure_foundry.summary: Sentinel hunting queries over the workspace are the data surface; a Foundry deployment generates hypotheses against summarized results rather than raw logs. Promote validated hunts to analytics rules.

google_vertex_ai.summary: SecOps search over the unified telemetry is the data surface; promote a validated hunt into a detection rule so the outcome persists.

title: Predictive threat analytics in use
summary: Models forecast likely attack patterns based on telemetry trends.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Time-series forecasts on attack telemetry. Models retrained on a defined cadence.

summary: Production models retrain on a schedule with A/B comparison and rollback.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Versioned datasets, versioned models, holdout eval sets. A/B traffic via the inference gateway.

aws_bedrock.summary: SageMaker Pipelines with Model Monitor drives the retraining trigger; Bedrock Custom Models supports versioned fine-tune deployments. A/B traffic split via inference gateways or Bedrock endpoint routing.

azure_foundry.summary: Azure ML model monitoring detects data and prediction drift and can trigger the retraining pipeline; the registry holds the versions that A/B traffic splits between.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Model monitoring detects drift and triggers the retraining pipeline; Model Registry holds the versions, and traffic splitting across endpoint versions carries the A/B.

aws_bedrock.summary: Security Hub dashboards exported to QuickSight feed the quarterly board pack. Snapshot the same metrics each quarter for trend comparability.

azure_foundry.summary: Defender for Cloud secure score and the AI posture findings give the quantitative trend line; snapshot the same query each quarter so the board sees change rather than a new metric each time.

title: AI ethics board or review process in place
summary: An ethics review function evaluates high-stakes AI decisions independently of product owners.

cloud_agnostic.summary: External members on the panel for credibility. Public summary of decisions.

title: Bias and fairness monitoring operational
summary: Production AI systems are continuously evaluated for bias against defined fairness criteria.

cloud_agnostic.summary: IBM AIF360, Fairlearn, or custom evaluation harnesses against held-out demographic data.

aws_bedrock.summary: SageMaker Clarify for both pre-training data bias and post-training prediction bias, with Model Monitor for drift over time. Findings to Security Hub.

azure_foundry.summary: The Responsible AI dashboard covers fairness assessment and error analysis, and the scorecard turns a run into a shareable artifact for the review body. Model monitoring tracks drift between runs.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Model monitoring tracks feature and prediction skew over time, and the evaluation service scores against the fairness criteria you define. Both attach to the model version.

title: Reasoning traceability and decision audit artifacts
summary: For each high-stakes AI decision, the reasoning chain is retained and auditable.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Trace IDs link to retrieval context, tool calls, and intermediate outputs. Retention aligned to regulatory and contractual requirements.

aws_bedrock.summary: Bedrock invocation logs (request, response, guardrail decision) plus CloudTrail data events (who called what model when) plus AgentCore traces (every tool step). Stream into a single CloudWatch Logs group with retention aligned to regulatory requirements.

azure_foundry.summary: Foundry observability retains per-run traces including retrieval context and tool steps; pair with the resource activity log for who invoked what, and set retention on the workspace to the regulatory requirement.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Data Access audit logs record who invoked which model when, the agent runtime retains per-step traces, and ML metadata links the run back to the model version. Set sink retention to the regulatory requirement.

title: Formal NHI lifecycle management with automated credential rotation and decommissioning
summary: Agent NHIs are provisioned, rotated, and decommissioned through automation tied to the asset register.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Vault dynamic secrets or SPIFFE workload identity with automated rotation. Decommission ties to the asset-register lifecycle.

aws_bedrock.summary: IAM Identity Center for human-tied agent ownership. AgentCore Identity for the agent itself, with credential rotation tied to the agent lifecycle and an AWS Config rule that flags AgentCore identities older than the rotation window.

azure_foundry.summary: Managed identities remove the rotation problem for anything Entra can authenticate; for the rest, Key Vault with a rotation policy. Decommissioning is a role-assignment removal, so tie it to the asset register's owner column.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Workload identity federation removes exported keys entirely, which removes most of the rotation problem. Decommissioning is a service account deletion plus binding removal, driven from the register.

title: Self-improving AI defenses
summary: Defenses adapt their detections and controls based on continuous adversarial feedback.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Closed-loop: red-team output flows into detection authoring with measured time-to-coverage.

title: Autonomous adversarial detection operational
summary: Novel adversarial techniques are detected by the system without human pre-definition.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Anomaly-on-anomaly approaches against agent behavior baselines. Requires sustained eval infrastructure.

title: AI system chaos engineering conducted continuously
summary: Chaos exercises validate resilience of agentic systems under fault, latency, and adversarial conditions.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Litmus or Chaos Mesh applied to AI inference stacks. Adversarial chaos in addition to fault chaos.

title: Zero Trust architecture fully extended to autonomous AI agents with context-aware, JIT permissions
summary: Agent authorization is computed per request, with just-in-time elevation and consequence-based gating.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Cedar/OPA policies with request context and consequence rating. Synchronous human approval reserved for irreversible or high-impact actions.

aws_bedrock.summary: AgentCore Identity with per-request session policies and IAM Roles Anywhere for cross-environment workload identity. Cedar evaluates the consequence ladder per action.

azure_foundry.summary: Compute authorization per request rather than per agent: Conditional Access on the calling identity, a narrowly scoped role assignment for the ceiling, and a check in the tool path that carries the consequence rating for the specific action.

google_vertex_ai.summary: IAM conditions and the service perimeter set the ceiling; a request-time check in the tool path carries the consequence rating. Workload identity federation keeps cross-environment agents keyless.

title: AI systems demonstrate antifragile properties
summary: Failures and attacks produce systemic improvements rather than degradation.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Postmortem outputs feed automated detection and policy updates; measured time-to-improvement is the KPI.

title: Continuous AI security validation
summary: Validation against the full ATLAS matrix runs continuously, with novel-technique discovery measured as a metric.

cloud_agnostic.summary: Continuous Garak / custom-suite runs as a service, dashboards per AI system.

aws_bedrock.summary: Scheduled Bedrock model evaluation jobs against a continuously expanding adversarial suite. Findings publish to Security Hub for trend visibility.

azure_foundry.summary: Schedule the red teaming agent against every deployed endpoint and keep the scores in one workspace, so novel-technique discovery reads as a trend rather than a set of one-off reports.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Schedule evaluation runs against every deployed model and route the scores and Model Armor findings into Security Command Center, so validation lands beside the rest of the security signal.

title: AI agents authorized for Level 1 remediation
summary: Validated agents perform Level 1 incident response actions autonomously, with human review for exceptions.

cloud_agnostic.summary: L1 scope tightly defined and audited. Out-of-scope actions deny by default with escalation.

aws_bedrock.summary: AgentCore agents scoped to L1-only actions with explicit allow-lists and Guardrails. Out-of-scope tool calls deny with escalation to the on-call human via PagerDuty or AWS Chatbot.

azure_foundry.summary: Scope the agent's managed identity to the Level 1 action set only and let the deny be the escalation path: an out-of-scope call fails at the role assignment and raises a Sentinel incident rather than silently succeeding.

google_vertex_ai.summary: Scope the agent's service account to the Level 1 action set only. An out-of-scope call fails at IAM and surfaces in audit logs, which is the escalation trigger.

title: Self-healing security infrastructure operational
summary: Configuration drift, control failure, and policy violation are remediated automatically with notification.

cloud_agnostic.summary: GitOps + policy-as-code with automated remediation tied to known-good baselines.

azure_foundry.summary: Azure Policy remediation tasks return drifted resources to the baseline automatically, with compliance state as the notification surface and Defender for Cloud posture as the check that it worked.
